original_question: Fix d and let D_d be a Jordan measurable domain of volume 1. For the classical smoothness classes F_d^k(D_d), does the asymptotic constant C_{D_d} = lim_{n->infinity} e(n,F_d^k(D_d)) n^{k/d} exist, and if it exists, is it independent of the particular shape of D_d, perhaps under suitable assumptions on the boundary?
target_in_paper: Section 4 ("General Domains"), subsection "Asymptotic Constant and Explicit Uniform Bounds", specifically Remark 7(2), together with the immediately preceding definition of the classes F_d^k(D_d). This is an unnumbered guess/open question, not a formal numbered conjecture.
correct_elements: Your draft already captures the paper's actual target very closely: it fixes d, considers unit-volume Jordan measurable domains D_d, uses the classical smoothness classes F_d^k(D_d), asks about the existence of the limit lim_{n->infinity} e(n,F_d^k(D_d)) n^{k/d}, and asks whether that constant is independent of the shape of D_d, possibly under additional boundary assumptions. That is essentially Remark 7(2) rewritten in your own words.
missing_details: k should be explicitly fixed as a positive integer; the asymptotic constant depends on k as well as on d, so writing only C_{D_d} hides that dependence.
The class should be defined exactly as F_d^k(D_d) = {f : D_d -> R | ||D^alpha f||_{L_infty(D_d)} <= 1 for every multi-index alpha in N_0^d with |alpha| <= k}.
The problem is specifically numerical integration: e(n,F_d^k(D_d)) is the nth minimal worst-case error for approximating the integral f -> integral over D_d of f(x) dx using n function values.

The ambient setting is real-valued functions on subsets D_d of R^d; multi-index notation alpha in N_0^d, |alpha| = alpha_1 + ... + alpha_d, and D^alpha as the corresponding partial derivative are implicit in the paper and should be made explicit in a stand-alone version.

The nearby context matters: the paper first notes that the weak order e(n,F_d^k(D_d)) approx n^(-k/d) is known at least for bounded Lipschitz domains; the open question is whether one can sharpen this to a domain-independent exact asymptotic constant for Jordan measurable unit-volume domains.
The paper phrases this as a guess in Remark 7(2), not as a theorem or a numbered conjecture.

There is a small implicit regularity issue: Remark 7(2) says 'Jordan measurable' while the derivative-based class F_d^k(D_d) is most naturally interpreted on open domains, so any fully self-contained restatement should either keep 'domain' or explicitly say how derivatives on D_d are understood.
refined_question: Fix integers d,k >= 1. Let D_d be a Jordan measurable domain in R^d with lambda_d(D_d) = 1, and define F_d^k(D_d) = {f : D_d -> R | ||D^alpha f||_{L_infty(D_d)} <= 1 for every multi-index alpha in N_0^d with |alpha| <= k}. If e(n,F_d^k(D_d)) denotes the minimal worst-case error of numerical integration f -> integral over D_d of f(x) dx based on n function values, then it is known at least for bounded Lipschitz domains that e(n,F_d^k(D_d)) has order n^(-k/d). Is it true that, for fixed d and k, the exact asymptotic constant C_{d,k}(D_d) := lim_{n->infinity} e(n,F_d^k(D_d)) n^{k/d} exists and is independent of the particular domain D_d whenever D_d is Jordan measurable with lambda_d(D_d) = 1, possibly after imposing suitable assumptions on the boundary of D_d?
justification: The draft matches Remark 7(2) almost verbatim. In Section 4, Novak first frames the general issue of exact asymptotic constants once an order of convergence is known. He then turns to the classical C^k-type classes, recalls the general-domain version of F_d^k(D_d) and the known lower bound for unit-volume domains, and immediately states in Remark 7(2) that the weak order e(n,F_d^k(D_d)) approx n^(-k/d) is known at least for bounded Lipschitz domains, but that he expects more: the limit lim_{n->infinity} e(n,F_d^k(D_d)) n^{k/d} should not depend on D_d (for fixed d) when D_d is Jordan measurable with lambda_d(D_d)=1, possibly under boundary assumptions. Section 1 supplies the meaning of e(n,F_d) as the minimal worst-case n-sample integration error. So the nearest paper-faithful target is exactly this remark, not a broader problem about arbitrary smoothness spaces or unrelated asymptotic constants.
